topic: Principles of Cell Biology and Organization
summary: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. This module explores cell theory, the differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, organelle functions, and the levels of organization from tissues to organ systems.

subtopics.title: Cell Theory and Structure
keyPoints: Cells arise only from the division of existing cells
All living things are composed of one or more cells
Eukaryotic cells are compartmentalized and roughly ten times larger than prokaryotes
The cell membrane is a fluid mosaic consisting of 45 percent protein, 45% lipid, and 10% carbohydrate
definitions: Cell: The basic unit of structure and function in living things
Intrinsic Proteins: Proteins that span the entire width of the cell membrane
Organelles: Small membrane-bound units within a cell that perform specialized functions
processes: Membrane Transport: Materials move via diffusion, osmosis, active transport, endocytosis, and exocytosis
Independent Existence: The ability of solitary cells to survive alone under suitable conditions
examTraps: Assuming all cells have mitochondria (only Eukaryotes do)
Confusing colonial organisms where cells survive alone with multicellular organisms where specialized cells cannot
possibleQuestionPoints: Comparison of DNA location in prokaryotes vs eukaryotes
Role of cholesterol in membrane fluidity
Function of the mitochondrial cristae and matrix
mustKnow: Robert Hooke first recorded cell observations in 1663 using cork
The cell membrane is self-sealing and can divide without bursting

subtopics.title: Levels of Organization and Tissues
keyPoints: Cells performing the same function form tissues
Grouped tissues form organs, and grouped organs form systems
There are eleven major organ systems in vertebrates
definitions: Tissue: A group of connected cells with the same structure and function
Epithelium: Sheet-like layers of cells covering body surfaces and internal cavities
Extracellular Fluid (ECF): The fluid environment bathing cells, containing required ions and nutrients
processes: Cellular Communication: Individual cells perform specialized functions coordinated by complex signaling systems
Bone Reshaping: Continuous process of mineral removal by osteoclasts and building by osteoblasts
examTraps: Thinking the pancreas belongs to only one system (it is both endocrine and digestive)
Assuming all connective tissue is hard (blood is a fluid connective tissue)
possibleQuestionPoints: Types of epithelial cell shapes: squamous, cuboidal, and columnar
The six major types of vertebrate connective tissue
Structural unit of bone known as the osteon
mustKnow: H, O, C, and N make up over 99 percent of atoms in the human body
Epithelial tissues protect against bacterial and viral invasion

topic: Macromolecules and the Chemistry of Life
summary: Biological phenomena are governed by the chemistry of four major classes of macromolecules: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Their structures determine their specific biological functions.

subtopics.title: Biomolecular Hierarchy and Interactions
keyPoints: Simple molecules serve as units for building complex metabolites and macromolecules
Weak chemical forces like hydrogen bonds and van der Waals interactions mediate biomolecular recognition
Biopolymers are directional and built from chiral monomers
definitions: Polymer: A long molecule consisting of many similar building blocks called monomers
Chirality: The geometric property of molecules being non-superimposable on their mirror images
Denaturation: The loss of a protein's native conformation due to environmental changes like pH or temperature
processes: Dehydration Reaction: Synthesis of a polymer by removing a water molecule
Hydrolysis: Breakdown of a polymer by adding a water molecule
examTraps: Classifying lipids as polymers (they are macromolecules but do not form long monomer chains)
Assuming denaturation destroys the primary sequence of amino acids (it affects 3D shape only)
possibleQuestionPoints: Energy levels of different weak bonds
The role of chaperonins in protein folding
Directionality of a polypeptide (N-terminus to C-terminus)
mustKnow: A single amino acid substitution causes Sickle-cell disease
Proteins account for more than 50 percent of the dry mass of most cells

subtopics.title: Structure and Function of Major Classes
keyPoints: Carbohydrates serve as fuel and structural material
Lipids are hydrophobic and include fats, phospholipids, and steroids
Nucleic acids store and transmit hereditary information
definitions: Glycosidic Linkage: The covalent bond joining two monosaccharides
Saturated Fat: A fat with the maximum number of hydrogen atoms and no double bonds
Nucleotide: Building block of nucleic acids consisting of a base, sugar, and phosphate
processes: Protein Conformation: The twisting and folding of polypeptides into a unique functional shape
X-ray Crystallography: A method used by scientists to determine a protein's 3D structure
examTraps: Confusing alpha-glucose (helical starch) with beta-glucose (straight cellulose)
Missing that RNA uses Uracil while DNA uses Thymine
possibleQuestionPoints: Difference between purines and pyrimidines
Components of sucrose, maltose, and lactose
Structural roles of chitin in arthropods and fungi
mustKnow: DNA exists as an anti-parallel double helix
The four levels of protein structure: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, and Quaternary

summary: Bioenergetics focuses on energy transformations in living cells. It details how organisms acquire and utilize energy through metabolic pathways to perform biological work.

subtopics.title: Thermodynamics and Free Energy
keyPoints: Energy transformations obey the laws of thermodynamics
Cells are isothermal systems functioning at constant temperature and pressure
ATP is the primary energy currency of the cell
definitions: Bioenergetics: The study of energy changes in biological reactions
Exergonic: A spontaneous reaction that releases free energy (negative Delta G)
Endergonic: A non-spontaneous reaction requiring energy input (positive Delta G)
processes: Metabolism: The sum of all catabolic (breakdown) and anabolic (synthesis) reactions
Oxidative Phosphorylation: The process of synthesizing ATP when ADP levels are high
examTraps: Confusing enthalpy (heat content) with entropy (disorder)
Assuming a reaction at equilibrium (Delta G = 0) can perform work
possibleQuestionPoints: Application of the Gibbs Free Energy equation
Energy charge and the ATP/ADP ratio
Characteristics of high-energy compounds (liberating at least 7 Cal/mol)
mustKnow: First Law of Thermodynamics: Energy cannot be created or destroyed
Second Law of Thermodynamics: The entropy of the universe always increases

subtopics.title: Cellular Respiration Pathways
keyPoints: Respiration combines oxygen with glucose to release energy
Glycolysis is an anaerobic process occurring in the cytosol
Aerobic respiration yields significantly more ATP than anaerobic pathways
definitions: Glycolysis: The breakdown of one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules
Fermentation: The process following glycolysis when oxygen is absent to regenerate NAD+
Krebs Cycle: A series of reactions in the mitochondria producing energy-storing molecules
processes: Stage 1: Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate
Stage 2: The Krebs cycle and Electron Transport Chain produce the bulk of cellular ATP
examTraps: Thinking glycolysis happens in the mitochondria (it occurs in the cytoplasm)
Miscounting the net ATP gain of glycolysis (net gain is 2 ATP)
possibleQuestionPoints: Products of the Krebs Cycle
The role of oxygen as the final electron acceptor
Comparison of aerobic vs anaerobic energy yields
mustKnow: Carbon dioxide and water are the waste products of respiration
Enzymes like PFK regulate the steps of glycolysis

summary: This topic covers the principles of heredity established by Mendel and the molecular mechanisms of the Central Dogma, including DNA replication, transcription, and translation.

subtopics.title: Mendelian Genetics
keyPoints: Genes are carried on chromosomes and occur in pairs
Traits are determined by dominant and recessive alleles
Sexual reproduction creates new combinations of genes through fertilization
definitions: Genetics: The branch of biology dealing with heredity and variation
Allele: Different versions of a gene for the same trait
Dihybrid Cross: A mating involving parents that differ in two independent traits
processes: Segregation: Mendel's principle that alleles separate during gamete formation
Test Cross: Breeding an organism of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive individual
examTraps: Confusing phenotype (outward appearance) with genotype (genetic makeup)
Applying the 3:1 ratio to a dihybrid cross instead of a monohybrid cross
possibleQuestionPoints: Mendel's seven traits in pea plants
Calculating probabilities of genetic disorders like Gaucher Disease
Determining F2 phenotypic ratios (9:3:3:1 for dihybrid crosses)
mustKnow: Gregor Mendel is the father of modern genetics
Pure lines were used for eight years to establish basic genetic laws

subtopics.title: The Central Dogma and Gene Expression
keyPoints: DNA stores genetic information, which is transcribed to RNA and translated into proteins
The genetic code is written in triplets called codons
Mutations are heritable changes in the DNA sequence
definitions: Transcription: Synthesis of mRNA using a DNA template strand
Translation: The process of building proteins at the ribosome using mRNA instructions
Anticodon: A triplet of bases on tRNA complementary to an mRNA codon
processes: DNA Replication: Semi-conservative process where DNA unwinds to form a replication fork
Protein Synthesis: Initiation, elongation, and termination stages at the ribosome
examTraps: Synthesizing mRNA in the 3' to 5' direction (mRNA is synthesized 5' to 3' using a 3' to 5' template)
Assuming all mutations are harmful (some are silent or beneficial)
possibleQuestionPoints: Differences between the leading and lagging strands
The role of DNA Polymerase and Helicase
The 64 possible codons and the 3 stop signals (UAA, UAG, UGA)
mustKnow: The start codon is always AUG, coding for Methionine
Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs)

summary: Embryology explores the prenatal development of organisms. It details the timeline from fertilization to the formation of complex structures and organ systems.

subtopics.title: Early Embryonic Events
keyPoints: The embryonic period covers the first eight weeks of development
Basic body plans and major structures are established during this phase
Cleavage involves rapid mitotic divisions without significant cell growth
definitions: Zygote: The single cell formed by the fusion of sperm and ovum
Morula: A 16-cell mass that enters the uterus roughly 96 hours post-fertilization
Gastrulation: Reorganization of the blastula into a three-layered gastrula
processes: Fertilization: Typically occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube
Implantation: The process where the blastocyst attaches to the uterine wall, completed by day 11
examTraps: Confusing the trophoblast (forms placenta) with the inner cell mass (forms embryo)
Misidentifying the location of fertilization as the uterus instead of the fallopian tube
possibleQuestionPoints: The three germ layers and their structural derivatives
The transition from morula to blastocyst
Specific days associated with cleavage stages
mustKnow: Genetic sex is determined at the time of fertilization
By the end of week 8, the embryo has all adult structures in precursor form

subtopics.title: Fetal Development and Support
keyPoints: The fetal period extends from week 9 until birth (week 38)
The placenta serves as the interface for nutrient and waste exchange
Fetal circulation is distinct from adult circulation
definitions: Decidua: The modified endometrial lining of the uterus during pregnancy
Placenta: A discoid organ responsible for nourishing the fetus
Amnion: The innermost membrane enclosing the watery environment of the fetus
processes: Organogenesis: The production and development of organs from germ layers
Placentation: The formation and arrangement of the placenta in the uterus
examTraps: Assuming the umbilical vein carries deoxygenated blood (it actually carries oxygenated blood to the fetus)
Confusing the chorion with the amnion
possibleQuestionPoints: Structure of the placental villi and intervillous space
The role of the umbilical cord
Growth milestones during the 17-20 week period
mustKnow: The fetal period is primarily characterized by growth and maturation
The umbilical vein carries O2 and nutrients, while arteries carry CO2 and waste

summary: Bioethics provides the framework for balancing the benefits and risks of biological research. Scientific integrity demands intellectual honesty and responsibility from researchers and institutions.

subtopics.title: Principles of Bioethics
keyPoints: Bioethics guides behavior in biomedicine and biotechnology
Moral judgments are often influenced by cultural and religious beliefs
Four major ethical systems include Natural Law, Proportionalism, Consequentialism, and Pragmatism
definitions: Autonomy: Respect for a rational individual's right to make un-coerced, informed decisions
Beneficence: The obligation to identify and maximize benefits for others
Non-maleficence: The fundamental duty to do no harm
processes: Ethical Decision Making: Using structured tools to resolve dilemmas in medicine and agriculture
Informed Consent: Ensuring individuals understand risks before participating in research or consuming GMOs
examTraps: Thinking bioethics only applies to medicine (it also covers environment and agriculture)
Confusing justice (fair treatment) with beneficence (doing good)
possibleQuestionPoints: The four principles of bioethics
Ethical concerns surrounding GMOs and cloning
The scope of research involving human subjects
mustKnow: Justice ensures fair treatment and equity through reasonable dispute resolution
Bioethics is necessary because economic incentives are not enough to protect public health

subtopics.title: Scientific Integrity and Misconduct
keyPoints: Scientific integrity is both an individual commitment and an institutional responsibility
Institutions must promote an environment of trustworthiness and lawfulness
Codes of conduct provide shared standards and positive support for ethical action
definitions: Fabrication: Making up data or information at any stage of the scientific process
Falsification: Manipulating research materials or results to inaccurately represent a record
Plagiarism: Appropriating another person's ideas or words without credit
processes: Peer Review: Ensuring fairness and accuracy in the reporting of scientific findings
Humane Animal Care: Adhering to ethical standards in research involving living subjects
examTraps: Assuming plagiarism only refers to direct word-for-word copying (it also includes ideas and processes)
Thinking fabrication and falsification are the same (fabrication is making up data; falsification is altering it)
possibleQuestionPoints: Elements of integrity in research
The role of codes of conduct in professional life
Consequences of ethical failure in the biotech industry
mustKnow: Intellectual honesty is the core requirement for proposing and reporting research
Transparency in conflicts of interest is essential for maintaining scientific credibility
